tldr: This paper shows that in offline RL, we should stop jointly training the actor and critic. Simply training the actor with behavior cloning (BC), freezing it, and reranking multiple candidate actions at inference time using a critic substantially outperforms conventional offline RL methods.
hero_caption: Comparison of average success rates across 30 offline goal-conditioned RL tasks. Decoupled methods (blue) that freeze the actor with BC and rerank candidates at inference time using a critic consistently and significantly outperform conventional coupled training baselines (grey), regardless of the critic type.
overview:
In offline reinforcement learning (Offline RL), jointly training the actor (action policy) and the critic (action-value estimator) has long been the standard recipe. But in a fixed-dataset regime where no new data can be collected, is this coupled training really optimal?

The authors revisit this fundamental question and identify two pathologies in the conventional approach. The first is an "out-of-distribution (OOD) amplification loop," where the actor drifts toward unknown actions that happen to be overestimated by the critic, which further exacerbates value overestimation. The second is a "support-value trade-off," where constraints that keep actions close to the data conflict directly with optimizing for high value. Under coupled training, the actor is forced to update under this inherent contradiction.

To solve this, the authors propose Decoupled Policy Extraction, which completely separates policy improvement (value maximization) from actor training. The actor is trained solely via behavior cloning (BC) to model the dataset's action distribution and then completely frozen. At test time, the BC actor generates multiple candidate actions, and an independently trained critic scores and reranks them to pick the single best action.

Evaluated on 30 tasks from the continuous control benchmark OGBench, this approach overwhelmingly outperforms conventional coupled methods like IQL and TRL. Remarkably, even with a naive, vanilla Q-learning critic without any anti-overestimation penalties, it achieves state-of-the-art performance. Thanks to batch parallelization, the inference latency stays below 0.53 ms, making this a practical breakthrough ready to be integrated into today's large robot foundation models.
contributions: Empirically identifying the mechanisms behind the "OOD amplification loop" and the "support-value trade-off" caused by conventional coupled actor-critic training in offline RL.

Systematizing the "Decoupled Policy Extraction" framework, where the actor is dedicated solely to candidate generation via behavior cloning and frozen, while an independent critic reranks candidates at inference time.

Demonstrating consistent and substantial improvements over major baselines like IQL and TRL across 30 OGBench tasks, and showing that even a naive Q-learning critic performs remarkably well under this paradigm.
Showing that batch-parallel proposal generation and critic evaluation keep inference latency under 0.53 ms with near-constant GPU memory usage, proving its readiness for real-time robotic control.

sections.heading: Why shouldn't the actor be trained by the critic in offline RL?
sections.summary: While mutual updates between actor and critic work well in online RL, coupled training causes harmful error amplification in offline settings with fixed data. This work proposes a new paradigm that decouples policy improvement from actor training, shifting it to inference-time reranking.
sections.details:
Standard actor-critic methods update the actor (policy) under the guidance of the critic (value function), and the improved actor interacts with the environment to collect fresh data. This self-correcting feedback loop is why coupled learning functions beautifully in online RL.

In offline RL, however, the story changes completely because no new data can be collected. No matter how much the actor is updated, the training dataset remains fixed, giving no opportunity to validate or correct critic errors. Instead, two severe issues emerge:

- The OOD amplification loop: When the critic happens to overestimate unseen actions, the actor gets biased toward them, drifting further into out-of-distribution regions in a vicious cycle.
- The support-value trade-off: Enforcing strong regularization to suppress drift into unknown actions makes it difficult to select genuinely high-value actions supported within the data.

To address this, the paper proposes Decoupled Policy Extraction, which completely separates policy improvement (value maximization) from actor training. The actor is trained solely via behavior cloning (BC) to capture the dataset's action distribution, and its weights are frozen. At inference time, this BC actor produces multiple candidate actions, and an independently learned critic ranks them so the top action can be executed.

This decoupling completely breaks the feedback loop where critic errors distort the actor. On 30 goal-conditioned tasks, for example, switching from standard coupled IQL to this decoupled approach dramatically boosted the average success rate from 47.89% to 68.49%. Shifting policy improvement from training-time actor updates to inference-time selection proves far better suited for the offline regime.

captions.F1: Overall performance aggregated across 30 offline tasks. Regardless of whether the critic is trained via IQL, Q-Learning, or Transitive Q (TRL), the decoupled approach combined with BC (top three blue bars) substantially outperforms traditional coupled methods (middle grey bars) and pure BC (bottom).

sections.heading: Formulating goal-conditioned RL and proposal-and-selection
sections.summary: This section formalizes offline goal-conditioned RL and sets up the separation between critic learning and policy extraction. It clearly defines the inference-time decision mechanism as a proposal-and-selection framework.
sections.details:
This work considers goal-conditioned Markov Decision Processes where an action $a$ is selected given a state $s$ and a goal $g$. The state-goal pair is treated as a context $x=(s, g)$, and learning relies entirely on a fixed offline dataset $\mathcal{D}$.

A key perspective of this paper is the explicit separation between critic training and policy extraction. Let $\widehat{Q}^c(x, a)$ denote the learned action-value function from the critic. When selecting an action from a finite set of candidates, the absolute magnitude of the value estimate does not matter; only the relative ranking among candidates is essential.

The inference-time policy is formalized as a proposal-and-selection policy consisting of three components:

- Action proposal model $q(a \mid x)$: Samples $N$ action candidates $\{a_1, \ldots, a_N\}$ given context $x$. This method uses a frozen BC model $q_{\mathrm{BC}}$ trained solely to model the dataset's action distribution.
- Selector: Picks the candidate that maximizes the critic score $\widehat{Q}^c(x, a)$ via $\arg\max$.
- Candidate budget $N$: The number of action proposals evaluated at inference time. While $N=1$ corresponds to standard policy sampling, choosing $N > 1$ enables policy improvement at test time without modifying the proposal model itself.

This formulation mathematically clarifies the difference from conventional RL-trained actors, where critic-derived losses directly modify the actor's network weights.

sections.heading: Dissecting why coupled learning fails: two core pathologies
sections.summary: Through visualizations and experiments, the authors prove that the OOD amplification loop and the support-value trade-off genuinely occur in conventional methods that jointly update actor and critic. They also highlight why overly conservative regularization hurts performance.
sections.details:
To understand why conventional coupled actor-critic methods struggle, the authors conducted detailed diagnostic experiments along two dimensions.

### 3.1 Empirical Evidence of the OOD Amplification Loop
First, using methods without explicit overestimation suppression (CRR with advantage weighting and TD3 with action-regularized Q-maximization), they visualized action distribution drift in PCA space. The 95% confidence region of a BC model (BC95), which reflects the data support, served as the reference boundary.

Initially, about 5.8% of actions fell outside BC95 for all models. As training progressed, pure BC remained at 6.8%, but TD3 reached 16.8% and CRR drifted to a staggering 31.3% outside BC95. Furthermore, actions outside the support received higher critic advantages and Q-values. In other words, critic overestimation lured the actor outside the dataset distribution, which in turn distorted the critic further, verifying the destructive feedback loop in practice.

### 3.2 The Support-Value Trade-Off
Does adding conservative regularization (pessimism) resolve the issue? The authors tested CQL, a representative conservative method, across varying values of the conservatism coefficient $\alpha_{\mathrm{CQL}}$.

Increasing the penalty moderately suppressed Q-values for unseen actions, reduced the fraction outside BC95, and improved task success rates. Crucially, however, the point where out-of-support actions were minimized ($\alpha=2$) did not match the point where task success peaked ($\alpha=10$). When the penalty was pushed even higher, Q-values for both OOD actions and genuinely high-value data-supported actions were crushed, degrading the critic's ability to discriminate good actions and causing success rates to drop steeply.

Attempting to reconcile "staying within data support" and "maximizing value" inside a single actor objective is inherently flawed in principle.

captions.F2: Action distribution drift relative to the data support (dashed line: BC95 region). Compared to pure BC (left), coupled training methods CRR (middle) and TD3 (right) push actions far beyond the dashed boundary by the end of training (bottom row), with out-of-support regions receiving noticeably higher critic scores (darker shades).
captions.F3: Success rate (blue line) and BC95 violation rate (grey dashed line) across different CQL conservatism weights $\alpha$. The minimum violation point ($\alpha=2$) mismatches the peak performance point ($\alpha=10$), illustrating the trade-off where excessive regularization collapses value discriminability and hurts performance.

sections.heading: Decoupled training: freeze BC, learn a critic, and pick at test time
sections.summary: This section details the proposed method: training and freezing the BC actor, relaxing requirements on the critic, and controlling exploration simply via the test-time candidate budget $N$.
sections.details:
The design philosophy is straightforward: completely separate the responsibilities of the components.

### 4.1 Frozen BC Actor
First, using the offline dataset $\mathcal{D}$, the actor $q_\psi(a \mid x)$ is trained purely via behavior cloning (such as negative log-likelihood minimization or flow matching). Once trained, the actor parameters are completely frozen. Rewards, critic Q-values, and gradients are never backpropagated into the actor. This completely eliminates any risk of the actor drifting into unseen territory during training.

### 4.2 Relaxed Critic Requirements: Why Naive Q-Learning Works
In conventional offline RL, the critic must penalize every unseen action heavily across the entire action space (as in CQL or IQL) to stop the actor from selecting bad moves. Under the decoupled paradigm, however, all candidates evaluated at inference time are drawn directly from the BC actor, meaning they are already supported by the dataset.

Consequently, the critic does not need global pessimism across the entire action space; it only needs to correctly score the relative ranking among valid candidate actions. This provides a major benefit: even a naive, vanilla Q-learning critic without complex conservative regularization works exceptionally well.

### 4.3 Test-Time Policy Improvement via Reranking
During inference, the frozen BC actor samples $N$ candidates, the critic scores them, and the highest-scoring candidate is executed.

In conventional coupled methods, balancing data support and value improvement requires repeated hyperparameter sweeps and retraining. In contrast, this decoupled approach reduces the balancing act to a single lightweight inference-time knob: the candidate count $N$. Trade-offs between exploration and safety can be tuned on the fly without retraining the model.

sections.heading: Dominating 30 tasks: naive Q-learning beats IQL by a landslide
sections.summary: Evaluations across 6 environments and 30 tasks in OGBench show that the decoupled method substantially outperforms conventional baselines. Practical robotics aspects, such as the effect of candidate budget $N$ and sub-millisecond parallelized latency, are also verified.
sections.details:
### Experimental Setup
Evaluations were conducted on 6 environments from the continuous control benchmark OGBench (locomotion: AntMaze-Large, AntSoccer-Arena, HumanoidMaze-Medium; manipulation: Cube-Double, Scene-Play; visual/logic puzzle: Puzzle-4x4), totaling 30 tasks with 5 tasks per environment. Critic backbones included standard Q-Learning, expectile-regression-based IQL, and transition-based TRL, paired with Flow Matching (FM) generative models.

### Main Results
The results were striking. When using IQL as the backbone, the decoupled version (BC + IQL) surpassed standard coupled IQL by 38.4% on locomotion, 13.9% on manipulation, and an astounding 202.2% on puzzle tasks (Table 1).

Even more surprising, naive BC + Q-Learning outperformed IQL—the de facto standard in conservative offline RL—on many tasks. On the Puzzle environment in particular, Q-learning reranking showed a 212.8% improvement over IQL. Because IQL conservatively updates values using dataset actions to avoid OOD queries, value differences between optimal and mediocre actions get compressed in sparse-reward, long-horizon tasks, which degrades its ranking accuracy.

### Impact of Candidate Budget $N$ and Inference Cost
An ablation varying $N$ from 1 to 32 on Puzzle-4x4 (Figure F4) showed that performance peaked around $N=8 \sim 16$, plateauing or slightly dipping beyond that. When $N$ is too small, good actions are missed; when $N$ is too large, the critic can occasionally misidentify and select low-probability OOD actions lying in the tail of the BC distribution.

Regarding inference latency for real-world robotics, measurements on Cube-Double (Table 3) showed that batching $N$ candidate generations and critic evaluations resulted in a median latency under 0.53 ms even at $N=32$, with GPU memory holding virtually constant around 550 MiB. This comfortably meets real-time control requirements.

captions.F4: Success rate (vertical axis) versus candidate budget $N$ (horizontal axis) across Puzzle-4x4 tasks. Performance climbs sharply from $N=1$ (standard sampling) and peaks around $N=8\sim 16$.

sections.heading: Related work and positioning: the lineage of test-time improvement
sections.summary: This section reviews conventional coupled offline RL, inference-time optimization techniques, and the policy extraction bottleneck, highlighting the paper's contribution in formalizing these ideas into a generalized decoupled paradigm.
sections.details:
The history of offline RL has largely been a battle against extrapolation errors on unseen actions. Prominent methods such as BCQ, CQL, IQL, and AWAC, as well as recent diffusion- and flow-based RL algorithms, still mostly rely on coupled improvement where critic feedback directly updates the actor weights.

Meanwhile, inference-time policy improvement has been explored from various angles:

- Sample-and-select methods: Approaches like SfBC and EMaQ sample from an action model and pick with a critic, but their proposal models are tightly integrated into critic training rather than fully decoupled.
- Trajectory guidance methods: Frameworks such as Diffuser, QGF, and GAF guide actions using critic gradients during the generation process, keeping the generator tightly coupled with the critic.
- Early decoupled precursors: Algorithms like IDQL and V-GPS share similar architectural principles, but were presented within specific algorithmic or application-focused contexts.

This work advances the known insight that offline RL bottlenecks stem from policy extraction rather than value learning itself. It formalizes a general decoupled framework cleanly separating the proposal model, critic, selection rule, and search budget, while verifying the mechanisms behind its superiority through rigorous comparative experiments.

sections.heading: Major implications for the era of robot foundation models
sections.summary: This study challenges conventional wisdom in offline RL by establishing the superiority of decoupling policy improvement into test-time selection. It offers an efficient blueprint for scaling large robot foundation models using lightweight plug-in critics.
sections.details:
This paper offers a resounding "no" to the long-held assumption that actor training and policy improvement must happen simultaneously in offline RL. By shifting policy improvement to test-time reranking, the decoupled design neatly resolves both the OOD amplification loop and the support-value trade-off.

This finding holds practical implications for developing large robot foundation models, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) architectures.

Rather than fine-tuning massive, highly expressive models with unstable RL objectives, practitioners can train large models purely on imitation (BC) and keep them frozen. Task-specific optimization can then be delegated to lightweight, independently trained critics. A single foundation policy can thus be reused across tasks by swapping inexpensive critics at inference time, yielding an exceptionally scalable robotic system architecture.

A recognized limitation is that the critic can only select from actions proposed by the BC actor. Because it cannot generate actions entirely absent from the dataset, the proposal model's expressiveness and data coverage set the upper bound on performance. Nonetheless, this simple and effective approach challenges many existing, highly complex offline RL algorithms.

takeaways: In offline RL, keeping the actor frozen with BC rather than updating it with critic gradients or weights prevents error amplification and dramatically boosts performance.
Policy improvement does not need to happen during training; sampling multiple candidates at inference time and reranking them with a critic is entirely sufficient.
Because action proposals are restricted to data-supported regions, critics do not need heavy conservative penalties, allowing naive Q-learning critics to perform exceptionally well.
Batch-parallel candidate evaluation keeps inference latency around 0.5 ms, making the method immediately applicable to real-time physical robot control.
For future large-scale robot models (like VLAs), freezing the foundation model with BC and attaching lightweight, task-specific critics for test-time reranking represents a highly promising workflow.
limitations: Performance is strictly bounded by the data coverage of the BC proposal actor; optimal actions that are extremely rare or missing from the dataset cannot be proposed or selected.
Setting the candidate budget $N$ too high increases the risk that the critic erroneously selects out-of-distribution actions residing in the tails of the BC distribution.
While increasing $N$ can be parallelized in batches, total compute (FLOPs) still grows, presenting potential trade-offs in ultra-low-power embedded deployments.
